title: A new chip material for smaller, cooler power electronics
description: Researchers made a new chip material: a thin crystal film of aluminium, gallium and oxygen with a pinch of silicon added. Materials tough enough to withstand very high voltages usually block electricity completely, but this one still lets it flow. It grows on cheap wafers that factories already make in huge numbers, and two simple working electronic parts have been built from it.
capability: Power switches, the parts inside chargers, electric cars and the power grid that turn electricity on and off, could get smaller, run cooler and waste less energy. Researchers took a first step with a new lab-made chip material that should handle very high voltages and grows on cheap wafers factories already make. It's early lab work, not a product yet.
useCases: Smaller chargers and power supplies that stay cooler and waste less electricity as heat.
Electric cars, and the big computer centres that run the internet, losing less of their power as heat inside their electronics.
Grid equipment that moves solar and wind power to homes with less waste along the way.
body:
Inside every charger, electric car and power station, tiny switches turn electricity on and off to change it into the form a device needs, and each switch wastes a little energy as heat. Switches made from tougher materials, ones that can stand up to higher voltages, waste less and can be made thinner, and the gain grows very fast as the material gets tougher. The catch is that the toughest materials normally refuse to carry electricity at all. This film is tougher than any other material known to carry current in this controlled way, and among materials nearly this tough it carries current more than 100 million times better than any reported before. It grows on sapphire wafers, the same cheap crystal discs used to make LED lights and scratch-proof watch faces, instead of the tiny, costly crystals that rival materials such as diamond need.

It is still early lab work. The first parts built from it, a one-way valve for electric current and a simple switch, are proofs of concept, not products. Electricity still moves slowly through the film, only part of the added silicon actually helps carry current at room temperature, and a second, matching version of the material that most electronic parts also need has not been made yet.
